items.explanation: The Liberty League crowd denounced the New Deal on all three grounds: handouts for the undeserving, creeping Bolshevism, and strangling regulation.
options: A. It rewarded the undeserving
B. It smacked of Bolshevism
C. It overregulated business
D. All of the above
items.stem: Wealthy businessmen who opposed FDR's New Deal charged that

option_explanations.A: Opponents really did charge that the New Deal rewarded the undeserving — handouts to people they said should help themselves. This was a real charge, but only one of three.
option_explanations.B: Opponents really did charge that the New Deal smacked of Bolshevism — the Liberty League called it creeping socialism. This was a real charge, but only one of three.
option_explanations.C: Opponents really did charge that the New Deal overregulated business — strangling enterprise with federal rules. This was a real charge, but only one of three.
option_explanations.D: Correct — all three. Wealthy opponents, organized in the American Liberty League, denounced the New Deal on all three grounds: handouts for the undeserving, creeping Bolshevism, and strangling regulation of business.

items.explanation: After the 1933 bank holiday, the FDIC insured individual deposits in sound banks — restoring the confidence bank runs had destroyed.
options: A. Guarantee retirement income for the poor
B. Audit the books of major corporations
C. Insure individual bank deposits
D. Extend government control of the economy
items.stem: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created to

option_explanations.A: Guaranteeing retirement income was the job of Social Security (1935), not the FDIC. The FDIC dealt with banks, not pensions.
option_explanations.B: Auditing corporate books was the job of the Securities and Exchange Commission (1934), not the FDIC. The FDIC insured deposits; it did not audit corporations.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Created in 1933 after the bank holiday, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insured individual bank deposits in sound banks — restoring the public confidence that bank runs had destroyed.
option_explanations.D: The FDIC's purpose was narrower than 'government control of the economy' — it insured deposits to stop bank panics. It did not extend general economic control; that description misreads a confidence-restoring measure as a power grab.

items.explanation: Long's 'Share Our Wealth' and Coughlin's radio populism drew millions precisely because they said Roosevelt wasn't doing enough — pressure from the left, not the right.
options: A. The New Deal had gone too far
B. Americans were turning to religion
C. Americans wanted truly radical solutions
D. The government should do more to fight the Depression
items.stem: The popularity of Huey Long and Father Coughlin showed that

option_explanations.A: Long and Coughlin did not think the New Deal had gone too far — they attacked it from the left, saying it had not gone far enough. Their pressure was for more action, not less.
option_explanations.B: Coughlin was a priest, but the popularity of the two men was not about Americans turning to religion — it was about economic desperation. Long was a secular populist; their common ground was economic radicalism, not faith.
option_explanations.C: They did not call for truly radical solutions like revolution — Long's 'Share Our Wealth' and Coughlin's populism worked within the system. Their appeal showed demand for more government action, not for revolution.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Long's 'Share Our Wealth' and Coughlin's radio populism drew millions precisely because they said Roosevelt wasn't doing enough to fight the Depression — pressure from the left demanding the government do more, not from the right.

items.explanation: Townsend's pitch is in the passage: pension money 'put into circulation would so stimulate the productive ability of America.' The plan required the $200 to be spent within the month -- forced spending as economic stimulus. It promised no government savings, no wage hikes for the young, and no bank deposits.
options: A. Pensioners would have to spend the money immediately, stimulating production
B. The government would save money on relief programs
C. Young workers would earn higher wages
D. Banks would receive the pension funds as deposits
items.stem: According to the passage, Townsend argued his pensions would help the economy because
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"It would be quite impossible to start pensioning all of the old folks who have attained the age of 60 and have no means of support... The plan is obviously impractical and would do the country more harm than good."
—President Franklin D. Roosevelt, on the Townsend Plan (paraphrased)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Townsend's pitch, quoted in the passage, was that pension money 'put into circulation would so stimulate the productive ability of America.' The plan required the $200 to be spent within the month — forced spending as economic stimulus. The passage promises no government savings, no wage hikes for the young, and no bank deposits.
option_explanations.B: The passage promises no government savings — Roosevelt in fact calls the plan impractical and harmful. Saving money on relief was never Townsend's argument.
option_explanations.C: The passage says nothing about young workers earning higher wages. Townsend's argument was about pensioners spending money, not about raising the young's pay.
option_explanations.D: The passage says nothing about banks receiving pension funds as deposits — the money was to be spent immediately, which is the opposite of being saved in banks.

items.explanation: Roosevelt privately called pension demagogues like Townsend, Coughlin, and Long a political menace and moved to 'steal their thunder' -- his phrase -- by putting old-age insurance into the Social Security Act. The movements were rivals to be outflanked, not allies, and FDR took them very seriously indeed.
options: A. as a welcome ally of the New Deal
B. as a communist front to be suppressed
C. as a political threat to be outflanked with his own pension plan
D. as too marginal to deserve his attention
items.stem: Roosevelt viewed movements like Townsend's as
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"It would be quite impossible to start pensioning all of the old folks who have attained the age of 60 and have no means of support... The plan is obviously impractical and would do the country more harm than good."
—President Franklin D. Roosevelt, on the Townsend Plan (paraphrased)

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt did not see Townsend as a welcome ally — the passage shows him calling the plan 'obviously impractical' and harmful. The movements were rivals, not partners.
option_explanations.B: Roosevelt did not treat Townsend as a communist front to be suppressed — Townsend's movement was a populist pension crusade, not a communist one, and FDR's response was political outflanking, not suppression.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Roosevelt privately treated pension demagogues like Townsend, Coughlin, and Long as a political menace and moved to 'steal their thunder' — his phrase — by putting old-age insurance into the Social Security Act. The movements were rivals to be outflanked, and FDR took them very seriously.
option_explanations.D: Roosevelt did not consider the movement too marginal to notice — the passage and his political response show he took it as a serious threat worth answering with his own pension plan.
